turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Number 149! Really, Mr. Worthing, one would think you were attempting to be deliberately obscure. Does this Lady Bloxham, at the very least, possess a suitable pedigree? I insist on knowing everything.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma! Must you interrogate Mr. Worthing so relentlessly? It is exceedingly tiresome, and quite unnecessary, as I am already engaged to him.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Tiresome, my dear? Your sensibilities are as alarming as your precipitate declarations. I find it quite necessary to ascertain the gentleman's origins, and I shall not be deterred by frivolous complaints, Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mamma! Really, you are being quite dreadful. Must we endure this protracted examination when my happiness is already assured? I simply cannot understand why you persist in delaying the inevitable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Happiness, my dear Gwendolen, is not a matter to be 'assured' with such alarming haste. Mr. Worthing’s origins are of paramount importance, and I shall not allow sentimental declarations to distract me from the serious business of ensuring a suitable match. Pray, Mr. Worthing, let us proceed to question seventeen.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Question seventeen, Lady Bracknell? I… I confess, I'm not entirely certain what question seventeen pertains to. I do hope I haven’t missed something of vital importance.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your apparent bewilderment is… illuminating, though scarcely reassuring. Pray, do not imagine that I am conducting a mere frivolous pastime; the preservation of social order demands meticulous attention to detail, and that includes, apparently, numbering one's inquiries. Now, question seventeen concerns your professional standing; do enlighten me, sir, what occupation occupies your valuable time?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My occupation, Lady Bracknell? Well, I… I consider myself a gentleman of leisure, you see. I devote my time to various charitable endeavors and, of course, to cultivating the art of being agreeable.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A gentleman of leisure! How delightfully vague, Mr. Worthing. I trust this 'leisure' does not involve any… undesirable pursuits? One must, you see, maintain a certain decorum. Pray, elaborate upon these 'charitable endeavors'; I find I am quite intrigued.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My charitable endeavors, Lady Bracknell? I’m involved with the Foundling Hospital, assisting with… well, with various matters pertaining to the care of infants. It’s a most worthy cause, I assure you, and I find it quite fulfilling.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Infants, Mr. Worthing? A commendable sentiment, certainly, but hardly a substitute for a respectable profession. One would think a gentleman of leisure might possess some discernible skill, some… income, beyond the vague notion of being ‘agreeable.’ Pray, do not misunderstand me; I am not suggesting you are entirely devoid of merit, merely that further elucidation is… required.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Income, Lady Bracknell? Well, I have… resources, of course. I manage an estate in the country, you see, and it provides a modest, though entirely sufficient, income for my pursuits.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: An estate in the country, you say? How very… rustic. I trust, Mr. Worthing, that this estate is not burdened by any… ancestral complications? One simply *cannot* be too careful in these matters, you understand.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Ancestral complications, Lady Bracknell? Good heavens, I… I don’t believe so. My origins are… straightforward, really. I was found, you see, as a baby, in a handbag – a rather large handbag, I recall – and subsequently taken in by Mr. Jarvis.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Found in a handbag, Mr. Worthing? A handbag! Really! I must confess, I find that a most peculiar genesis for a gentleman. It suggests a lamentable lack of parental supervision, and a rather distressing disregard for established social decorum, wouldn't you agree?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A handbag, Lady Bracknell? Yes, quite extraordinary, I admit. But Mr. Jarvis was a man of impeccable character, and he assured me… well, he assured me my circumstances were perfectly… regular.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A handbag, you say? My dear Mr. Worthing, the impropriety of it all is simply staggering! One hardly knows whether to laugh or to express the deepest concern for the general welfare of society. Pray, elaborate further on this… handbag.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A handbag, Lady Bracknell? It was, as I recall, a rather fashionable handbag, actually—a black leather, with… with brass fittings. I believe my dear nurse, Miss Fair, used to admire it greatly; she said it was quite the height of fashion at the time.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A handbag! My dear Mr. Worthing, you appear to be determined to regale me with the minutiae of this… *incident*. Pray, does this fashionable handbag, with its brass fittings, possess any discernible family crest? For surely, a handbag of such significance must have belonged to someone of consequence.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: A family crest, Lady Bracknell? I… I don't believe it did, no. Miss Fair never mentioned a crest, and I’ve never seen one myself, to be honest. It was a rather… common handbag, I’m quite sure.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
